title: At the sea (Exodus 14)
hookLine: the army behind, water ahead; midrash says Nachshon walked in first

lines: WERE THERE NO GRAVES IN EGYPT?
cards: Freedom lasts about three days before Pharaoh changes his mind. Again. He takes six hundred of his best chariots and gives chase.
The Israelites are camped by the sea, and they look up and see the army coming. Water in front. Soldiers behind.
Nowhere to go. The people panic, and turn on Moses with one of the most bitter lines in the Torah: "Because there were no graves in Egypt, hast thou taken us away to die in the wilderness?"

teach.b: Moses answers with calm, well-known words: "Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD." It sounds perfect.

teach.h: SPEAK TO THEM, THAT THEY GO FORWARD.
teach.b: Then God says something surprising back: "Wherefore criest thou unto Me? speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward." Why are you crying out to me? Tell them to move.
Into the water? Moses lifts his staff, a strong east wind blows all night, the sea splits, "and the waters were a wall unto them on their right hand, and on their left."
But the rabbis noticed a gap between go forward and the sea splitting. Who moved first? The Talmud tells a story.
The tribes stood at the edge, each saying: I'm not going in first. You go.
Then one man, Nachshon, son of Amminadav, a prince of the tribe of Judah, walked into the sea. Up to his ankles.

teach.h: A WALL ON THE RIGHT AND THE LEFT.
teach.b: His knees. His waist. His neck.
The midrash says the water reached his nostrils, and only then did the sea split.

Another opinion in the same passage says the tribe of Benjamin jumped in first, and the Torah itself names no one. But Nachshon's story stuck: in modern Hebrew, a nachshon is someone who goes first, a pioneer.
The Israelites walk through on dry ground. The Egyptians follow, and the waters come back over them. The Torah says the people saw, and they believed.
But first somebody had to get their feet wet.

how: The crossing of the sea is read in synagogue on the seventh day of Passover, the day tradition says it happened, and on the Shabbat of the Song; Nachshon's story is a favorite in Jewish teaching about courage.

s: the Torah names Nachshon as the first into the sea
the Torah names no one. the story of Nachshon is from the Talmud and midrash.
God told Moses to stop crying out and tell the people to move
"Wherefore criest thou unto Me? speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward."

someone who goes first, after the man who walked into the sea.

games.q: you're at the edge of the sea. the army is coming. God has said go forward, but the water hasn't moved. every tribe is waiting for another to go first. what do you do?
o: wait for the sea to split.
games.why: the midrash says Nachshon walked in, up to his nose, and only then did the sea split.

practice: Think of something you're standing at the edge of: a hard conversation, an application, a doctor's appointment, a new start.
Notice the part of you waiting for the sea to split first, for the fear to go, for a sign, for someone else to go. Then picture the first step, just ankle deep, and see yourself taking it.

wordCard.voice: Nachshon. The prince of Judah who, the midrash says, walked into the sea first, while the people stood trapped between an army and the water.

orig.note: Hebrew: Nachshon, prince of Judah. in modern Hebrew, a pioneer, one who goes first.

carryVoice: Your line: walk in first. In the midrash, the sea split only once someone was in it. Day eighty-nine, done.
